Columbus Public Service Changes Due to Labor Day

No Trash, Recycling or Yard Waste Collection on Monday, Sept. 4

Trash Collection:

City of Columbus trash collection service will not be provided on Monday, Sept. 4, in observance of Labor Day.

For residents assigned a collection color, pickup will rotate forward by one day the week of the holiday:

Monday, Sept. 4:                        NO COLLECTION

Wednesday, Sept. 6:                 Gold

Friday, Sept. 8:                           Navy

Monday, Sept. 11:                      Pink

The color-coded trash collection schedule will rotate forward again on Friday, Nov. 10, in observance of Veterans Day.

For residents not assigned a collection color: If your collection day falls on or after the holiday, your trash pickup will be delayed by one day during the week of the holiday.

Recycling and Yard Waste Collection: Weekly recycling and biweekly yard waste service with a collection day that falls on or after the holiday will be delayed by one day during the week of the holiday, with Friday’s collection occurring on Saturday. 

Drop-Off Options: For recycling drop-off locations see https://recycleright.org/recycling locations/?category=49; for yard waste drop-off locations see https://new.columbus.gov/Services/Trash-Recycling-Bulk-Collection/Yard-Waste-Collection or contact the 311 Service Center online here, by email at 311@columbus.gov or at (614) 645-3111.

Parking Kiosks and Meters: Motorists may park free of charge at kiosks and meters on Monday, Sept. 4. Parking restriction signage at some kiosks and meters will be enforced, including but not limited to morning and evening rush hours and zones marked for valets, taxis, loading, handicapped-only and residential permit parking areas.

Offices Closed: Department offices, including the Parking Violations Bureau and the Right-of-Way Permits Office, will be closed on Monday, Sept. 4.  Permits may be filed online here.

item.title: City of Columbus to Extend Short North High Street Paid Parking to Midnight
item.description:
For Immediate Release

August 3, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

Short North On-Street Paid Parking Will Extend to Midnight to Support Safety, Access and Turnover 

The change will not affect the current hourly rate or residential permit parking streets

The City of Columbus will extend paid parking from 10 p.m. to midnight in the Short North on High Street, Goodale Street and side streets immediately off High to support safety, access and increased demand for late night parking. The current hourly parking rates will stay the same.

The extension to midnight from the existing paid parking time limits of 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. will be implemented by the Division of Mobility and Parking Services beginning on August 23. The new time limit will also impact Short North city-operated parking lots on Greenwood Avenue and Eden Alley.

“Extending paid parking to midnight on these high-demand streets will help to encourage turnover, particularly on the weekends when the Short North experiences more late night visitors and use of the High Street corridor curb lane,” said Justin Goodwin, Administrator of Mobility and Parking Services. “As always with adjustments made to on-street parking in the Short North Parking District, the intent is to support availability and access.”

These are the hourly parking rates, which are in effect currently and will not change, and the extended paid time limits effective August 23:

  • High Street and immediate side streets from Goodale Street to 9th Avenue – $1 per hour for 3 hours, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; $2 per hour 4 p.m. to midnight
  • Goodale Street – $1 per hour, 8 a.m. to midnight
  • The city Greenwood Avenue and Eden Alley parking lots – $1 per hour for 3 hours, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; $2 per hour 4 p.m. to midnight
  • Paid parking time restrictions on residential permit parking streets will remain unchanged, with permit only parking in place daily from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m.

"We appreciate the city's continued evaluation of parking solutions in the Short North," said Betsy Pandora, Executive Director of the Short North Alliance. "We have seen success with changes like this in the past and look forward to being able to welcome more visitors and ensure they have available parking any time they visit our neighborhood."

item.title: City of Columbus Offers Sustainability Services for OSU Move Out/Move In
item.description:
For Immediate Release

July 27, 2023

Contacts:

Debbie Briner, Columbus Department of Public Service; (614) 645-6467, dsbriner@columbus.gov

Dave Isaacs, The Ohio State University Office of Student Life; (614) 292-8424, Isaacs.84@osu.edu

Nora Gerber, University District Organization, (614) 610-4546 x200, noragerber@universitydistrict.org

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

 

City of Columbus to Continue Sustainability Collection Services for OSU Move Out/Move In

Furniture Bank of Central Ohio Is Participating to Collect Reusable Furniture Donations

Ohio State University students moving to and from off-campus housing before this fall semester can drop off recyclables and donate furniture and other households items at multiple neighborhood locations in the second year of a sustainability partnership between the City of Columbus, The Ohio State University Office of Student Life and the University District Organization.

This time, Furniture Bank of Central Ohio is  participating to collect reusable furniture, small appliances and household items for families in need. Other collection services provided by the Columbus Division of Refuse Collection during move out/move in include temporary dumpster and drop-off collection of recyclables and bulk items not suitable for reuse.

When the city added recycling collection  for the first time in 2022, students dropped off more than 6 tons of cardboard to divert it from the landfill. The sustainability services provided during move out/move in offer convenience to students and encourage reduce, reuse and recycle for a healthier environment.

“The city hopes to build on the success we had last year with students taking advantage of our expanded services to go green and reuse and recycle rather than unnecessarily landfilling items,” said Jennifer L. Gallagher, Director of the Columbus Department of Public Service. “Reducing the volume of waste and waste-generated greenhouse gas emissions benefits everyone in our community.”

The temporary Refuse Collection dumpsters and drop-off locations for bulk trash collection will be in place at 15 off-campus sites from Saturday, July 29, through Monday, August 14. Recycling dumpsters will be available at four of those sites.

In addition, Furniture Bank donations may be made at three of the locations from July 29 through August 1. See their donation standards at https://furniturebankcoh.org/donate-furniture/.

“The university appreciates the collaboration of our many partners to provide sustainability focused efforts,” said Rochelle Toth, Community Outreach and Engagement Manager at Ohio State’s Office of Student Life. “Involving our students not only prepares them to be sustainable citizens now and in the future, but also helps divert items from the landfills, having a positive impact on our entire community.”

"Many of the furniture pieces we see in the University District during move out/move in are still in good condition,” said Nora Gerber, Executive Director of the University District Organization. “This makes the new Furniture Bank donation sites a fantastic solution to redirect these items from the landfill to Columbus residents in need. We’re excited about this additional sustainable service and grateful for the ongoing collaboration with our partners to make this initiative a success."

This list identifies the Refuse Collection dumpster and drop-off locations available from July 29 through August 14 for bulk trash disposal of larger items such as furniture, mattresses and rugs; for recyclables collection; and where suitable Furniture Bank donations can be dropped off from July 29 through August 1.

  • 454 E. Northwood Ave., rear parking lot at Iuka Park Commons – plus recyclables collection
  • 176-178 E. Norwich Ave., rear parking lot
  • 117 W. Norwich Ave., side parking area
  • 1975 Summit St., rear parking area
  • 174 E. 12th, rear parking lot
  • 165 E. 11th, rear parking lot
  • 55 E. Blake Ave., side parking lot
  • 2351 W. Patterson Ave., next to Tuttle Pool – plus recyclables collection
  • 243-247 E. 18th, on-street dumpster
  • 28 E. Woodruff Ave., on-street dumpster – plus recyclables collection; Furniture Bank donations July 29 – August 1 only
  • 140 E. 16th, on-street dumpster; Furniture Bank donations July 29 – August 1 only
  • 1943 Waldeck Ave., on-street dumpster; Furniture Bank donations July 29 – August 1 only
  • 293 E. 14th, on-street dumpster
  • 225 E. 16th, rear on-street dumpster – plus recyclables collection
  • 1570 Highland St., on-street dumpster

For a map of these locations and other helpful move out/move in information, visit https://www.universitydistrict.org/move. And visit https://recycleright.org/ for information on acceptable items for the recycling dumpsters’ collection.

The on-street dumpster locations may require temporary parking restrictions. Students and others should pay attention to temporary No Stopping signage that may be in place and enforced around these locations.

item.title: City of Columbus Litter League 2023 Starts Soon
item.description:
For Immediate Release

May 22, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner, Department of Public Service

614-645-6467, dsbriner@columbus.gov

Contact: Aryeh Alex, Keep Columbus Beautiful

614-338--5004 

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

Columbus Litter League 2023 Starts Soon, Be a Team Player to Defeat Litter

The 2023 season of Litter League Columbus starts on June 1, and teams are forming now to knock out litter in city neighborhoods. Last season, more than 77,000 pounds of litter was cleaned up by participating players.

“Columbus Litter League demonstrates residents’ spirit to work together to wipe out litter in our community,” said Mayor Andrew J. Ginther. “With the support of returning sponsors Huntington Bank and the Columbus Clippers, we look forward to another successful season that inspires each of us to do our part in solving this unhealthy and unsightly issue.”

The 2023 Litter League season will operate the same as last year. Teams of up to 20 players each will compete in four divisions to pick up the most litter: corporate/business, nonprofit/faith-based, community groups and individuals. One bag of litter collected equals one run scored, and teams scoring the most runs during the season will win their division.

The season runs June 1 through August 31. Teams may choose where to do cleanups or get locations from Keep Columbus Beautiful, which manages Litter League.

“One of Huntington’s core principles is to strengthen the communities we serve, and our commitment to beautifying Columbus is second-to-none,” said Sue Zazon, Central Ohio Regional President for Huntington. “We are excited to work with community partners to make the upcoming Litter League season a grand slam!”

“We are once again proud to be a part of helping to gather litter in Columbus and team up with Huntington Bank to present The Litter League,” said Ken Schnacke, Clippers President and General Manager. “This is a great community program that does indeed make a difference. After all, the first image of any city is the cleanliness and neatness a visitor sees upon their arrival.”

The Litter League team scoring the most runs overall will play Wiffle ball at Huntington Park, home of the Clippers. Throughout their season, the Clippers will host Litter League special events at designated home games.

Register now to be a team player and score a win against litter in Columbus.

Keep Columbus Beautiful is the city’s community improvement program and national affiliate of Keep America Beautiful, focused on public education and volunteer service related to quality-of-life environmental issues including litter, recycling and beautification.

item.title: Keep Columbus Beautiful to Hold KickButt Columbus! on Saturday
item.description:
For Immediate Release

Date: March 9, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467; dsbriner@columbus.gov

Contact: Aryeh Alex, Keep Columbus Beautiful

614-338-5004 (cell)

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

KickButt Columbus! Will Tackle Cigarette Butt Litter on March 11

KickButt Columbus! volunteers will target several area highway ramps on Saturday, March 11, to clean up the most littered item in the country—cigarette butts.

The annual cleanup, managed by Keep Columbus Beautiful in the Department of Public Service, will pick up butts, paper, cans, bottles and other trash at dozens of entrance and exit ramps along I-70, I-71, SR 315 and SR 104, inside the I-270 outerbelt. More than 220 volunteers are already signed up to participate.

“The teamwork of KickButt Columbus! volunteers who roll up their sleeves to tackle litter in our community is inspiring,” said Mayor Andrew J. Ginther. “When we aggressively work to solve the issue of littering we are uplifting the wellbeing and health of our residents and the quality of our environment.”

The KickButt program raises awareness about the environmental damage caused when cigarette butts are tossed on the ground. In 2022, more than 200 KickButt Columbus! volunteers collected 14,757 pounds of butts and other litter discarded along the ramps. That equals the size of a large male elephant!

“The volunteer commitment to KickButt Columbus! demonstrates the pride residents have in our community,” said Jennifer L. Gallagher, Public Service Director. “We can solve litter by each of us doing our part to responsibly discard trash and prevent it from polluting our streets and waterways.”

You can still be a part of KickButt on Saturday by registering at keepcolumbusbeautiful@columbus.gov, or by calling 614-645-2421. Volunteers will meet at 9 a.m. at Wolfe Park, 105 Park Dr., Columbus, before dispersing to designated cleanup locations.

KickButt partners include Green Columbus, Friends of the Lower Olentangy Watershed, Friends of the Alum Creek Tributaries, Hashtag59, Clear Creeks and Byways and numerous other community groups, area commissions and nonprofit organizations.

For more information on Keep Columbus Beautiful and upcoming events, follow the program’s social media platforms including Facebook and Instagram.

item.title: City of Columbus to Begin 2023 Street Resurfacing Program
item.description:
For Immediate Release

March 7, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

City of Columbus Will Repave 59 Streets to Begin the 2023 Resurfacing Program

A capital investment of $9.76 million will fund the first round of neighborhood streets to be repaired and repaved in the City of Columbus annual street resurfacing program. The project will pave 59 streets and install 197 Americans with Disabilities Act-compliant curb ramps along these streets.

“The city’s annual resurfacing program delivers roadway improvements throughout our neighborhoods to ensure safe travel conditions on Columbus streets,” said Mayor Andrew J. Ginther. “We are proud to fund this important capital investment and to support the Department of Public Service, which provides pavement management expertise to maintain 5,700 lane miles of city streets.”

On Monday, City Council authorized a $9.76 million contract with Kokosing Construction Co. to perform the paving project beginning this spring. More streets are expected to be resurfaced in the 2023 program once another contract is bid and awarded and legislation is considered by City Council.

“The City of Columbus capital investment in street resurfacing means better and safer access for residents who walk, bike, roll, drive or use the bus along city streets,” said City Councilmember Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, chair of the Public Service and Transportation Committee. “This program impacts neighborhoods all around Columbus and is a feature of our annual capital improvements budget.”

Resurfacing of a street involves several steps by crews, including installing new ADA curb ramps and curb and sidewalk replacement for the ramps; milling existing pavement; making deep pavement repairs where needed; and laying the new pavement, first a tack coat to help asphalt adhere to the roadway and then the final asphalt layer.

Click here for the list and map of the 59 streets to be paved in the city’s Resurfacing – 2023 Project 1.

item.title: City of Columbus Will Reduce Downtown Speed Limit to 25 MPH
item.description:
For Immediate Release

February 7, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

City of Columbus Will Reduce Downtown Speed Limit to 25 MPH to Save Lives

The City of Columbus is reducing the speed limit to 25 miles per hour on Downtown District streets to enhance safety for all forms of transportation.

The lower speed limit, authorized by City Council on Monday, is a key Vision Zero Columbus strategy to reduce serious and fatal crashes on city streets, and to support safety as the top priority of the transportation system.

The Downtown District meets the Ohio Revised Code definition of a business district and gives the city jurisdiction to lower the speed limit on streets within it. The district is a core pedestrian area where many travel by walking, cycling or using transit on streets that often have high vehicle traffic.

“Slower vehicle speeds on our Downtown streets will save lives,” said Mayor Andrew J. Ginther. “This bold action advances our Vision Zero goal to eliminate all fatal and serious injury crashes on Columbus streets. The lower speed limit is especially supportive of safe and equitable travel by vulnerable road users who may not have access to a vehicle and must walk or bike to reach their destinations or a bus stop.”

Beginning later this month and into early March, the Department of Public Service, Division of Traffic Management will install 25 MPH Speed Limit signs throughout the Downtown District. Traffic signals will be retimed to support smooth traffic flow at the reduced speed limit.

In addition, the Leading Pedestrian Interval (LPI) safety feature is being implemented at seven Downtown signalized intersections to increase visibility of pedestrians crossing the street. LPI will give pedestrians a head start in the crosswalk, with the WALK signal displayed up to seven seconds before motorists making left or right turns at the intersection get a green light.

“Implementation Downtown of the reduced speed limit and enhanced crosswalk safety features embraces the Vision Zero principles to shift our approach toward slowing speeds, and to accommodate every user with safe access along our city streets,” said Jennifer L. Gallagher, Director of the Department of Public Service. 

LPI implementation is occurring at High St. at Rich St.; Broad St. at Cleveland Ave.; Mound St. at 3rd St.; 4th St. at Gay St.; Front St. at Mound St,; Grant St. at Town St.; and High St. at Mound St. Additional intersections will be considered as the first locations are monitored.

“Reducing the speed limit Downtown prioritizes safety over speed, and provides greater protection for those who are traveling on foot or by two wheels,” said City Councilmember Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, Chair of the Public Safety and Transportation Committee. “When a vulnerable road user is in a crash, a difference of 10 miles per hour in the speed limit may also be the difference between life and death.”

Lowering the speed limit Downtown is a safe streets strategy identified in the first Vision Zero Columbus Action Plan, adopted in 2021. Development of the second Action Plan is underway to identify and advance more strategies that prioritize safety on the city’s transportation system.

 A map of the Downtown District is available here.

item.title: Columbus Awarded $12 Million Safe Streets for All Grant for Livingston Ave
item.description:
For Immediate Release

February 1, 2023

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

City of Columbus Awarded a $12 Million Safe Streets for All Grant to Help End Serious Crashes on E. Livingston Avenue

The City of Columbus has been awarded a $12 million federal Safe Streets for All Implementation Grant to fund transportation safety improvements along E. Livingston Avenue in the Driving Park neighborhood. The grant, combined with a $12 million city investment, funds planning, design and construction of infrastructure changes that will make it safer to walk, bike and drive along Livingston — a corridor on the Vision Zero Columbus High Injury Network due to the high incidence of traffic violence.

The improvements will be made from 18th Street to Nelson Road. The Vision Zero safety project is focused on reducing pedestrian and fatal and serious injury crashes on Livingston.

The U.S. Department of Transportation announced the grant award today. The Livingston project is one of 510 projects across the U.S. to receive a historic $800 million in grant awards through the Safe Streets and Roads for All Grant Program, which funds regional, local and Tribal initiatives through grants to prevent roadway deaths and serious injuries.  

“I am grateful to the Biden administration, Transportation Secretary Buttigieg, Senator Brown and Congresswoman Beatty, and so many of our residents for their support of the Livingston Avenue project,” said Mayor Andrew J. Ginther. “This investment will significantly improve the safety and accessibility of the corridor, businesses and other community assets. It will help Driving Park and the surrounding neighborhoods reconnect with their rich histories and celebrate residents who made significant impacts on American history. Residents deserve the right to safe mobility.”

The Livingston project is led by the Department of Public Service, which is working with the neighborhood and a diverse steering committee of residents and business, faith and community organization representatives to plan and design corridor improvements.

“We understand residents’ concerns about the current Livingston roadway conditions that threaten pedestrian, cyclist and driver safety,” said Public Service Director Jennifer L. Gallagher. “Our partnership with the community is working toward real solutions to achieve a safe travel environment and connectivity for everyone who lives and travels along Livingston Avenue.”

Currently, the Public Service project team is working with residents on roadway design alternatives that will enhance safety at intersections, improve sidewalks and pedestrian crossings, provide protected bike lanes and reduce travel lanes to one in each direction, with a center turn lane to slow vehicle speeds and reduce crashes.

“The Safe Streets for All grant award is wonderful news and is desperately needed to reduce traffic violence in our neighborhood,” said Danielle Dillard, a Driving Park resident and member of the project steering committee. “The grant supercharges the city’s $12 million commitment to accessible, safe travel options along Livingston Avenue, reinvigorates our community and celebrates its spirit and history.”

Another public meeting on the project will be announced in the coming months. More information on the Livingston Avenue safety improvements project and the Safe Streets for All grant application can be found here.

Did you get a new computer or tablet this holiday season but aren’t sure how to dispose of the old one? The City of Columbus is hosting an environmentally friendly drop-off location to recycle electronics and divert them from the landfill.

The drop-off event will be held on Saturday, Dec. 31, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., at the Division of Refuse Collection facility at 2100 Alum Creek Dr., Columbus 43207.

The city encourages residents to reduce, reuse and recycle to achieve a healthier, more sustainable community, and to meet Columbus Climate Action Plan goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and the amount of waste generated.

The drop-off site will accept these electronics for recycling:

  • Desktops, laptops, servers, network equipment, hard drives and Chromebooks
  • Printers, copiers, fax machines and VCRs
  • Flat panel and LCD televisions and monitors
  • Tablets and mobile phones

CRT televisions and monitors and kitchen appliances will not be accepted. If you are dropping off cardboard, please break down large boxes. Bows and foil and metallic-like gift wrapping paper will not be accepted since they are not recyclable in the city’s residential program.

item.title: Columbus Department of Public Service Fall Newsletter
item.description:
From the Director's Desk

As we near the end of 2022, the Department of Public Service has much news to share about recent activities. Overall, it’s been a productive year of projects, planning and positive enhancements to essential city services you depend on. 

With winter weather impending, the Division of Infrastructure Management examined challenges our Snow Warriors faced in treating and plowing city streets during last February’s winter storm that brought heavy rain, then sleet and snow.  As a result, our snow plan has been upgraded to ensure snow plows service residential streets sooner during major snowfall, among other improvements. Read more below.

In other news, Scott Tourville recently was named Infrastructure Management Administrator, and Justin Goodwin is the new Administrator of the Division of Mobility and Parking, formerly known as Parking Services. The name change reflects the expanded approach of the division to holistically manage the curb lane for emerging mobility needs, along with parking and high demand for deliveries and passenger pickups and drop-offs.

Read more about Scott and Justin in this newsletter.

Also, I hope you take a minute to read the uplifting story below on our partnership with the Marysville Reformatory for Women. It’s about inspiring second chances, and an innovative approach by our Human Resources team to recruit and train more women for the Department’s workforce.

And, we have partnered with The Ohio State University to establish an endowment fund for scholarships to undergraduate engineering students, focused on building greater diversity on our engineering team and sparking students’ interest in working for the city.

Keep in touch with Public Service by following us on Facebook and Twitter. 

Wishing you a happy, healthy and peaceful holiday season!

City Plans to Deploy Plows In Neighborhoods Sooner During Snowfall This Winter

The Department has enhanced the city’s Snow and Ice Control Plan to get more plow trucks into neighborhoods sooner when heavy snowfall is forecasted this winter.

Using trained auxiliary city staff as operators, a pilot program will deploy plow-equipped pickup trucks to residential streets as soon as snowfall of 4 or more inches is predicted.

Other enhancements to the plan include upgrading 250 lane miles of residential streets to a higher priority to plow sooner for passable road conditions into and out of neighborhoods. And we have upgraded our digital Warrior Watch tool, which allows residents to check on the service status of their street during a winter weather event.

Each winter weather event is different, and climate change is impacting our winter temperatures and precipitation. The type and amount of precipitation falling in the winter may vary across our large city — Columbus covers approximately 225 square miles.

Our Snow Warriors treat and plow 4,700+ lane miles of city streets during winter weather events, including highways within Columbus, multi-lane arterial streets, rural-like roadways and urban and residential streets. Please be patient and don’t crowd the plows when they are at work on our roadways.

Learn more about the city’s Snow and Ice Control Plan.

East Livingston Avenue Road Diet Supports Safer Travel, Slower Speeds

This fall, our Division of Design and Construction reconfigured a section of Livingston Avenue, reducing it from four lanes of traffic — two eastbound and two westbound — to one travel lane in each direction with a center turn lane from College Avenue to James Road.

The road diet project also added median islands, improved crosswalks and traffic signals and resurfaced this section of Livingston. The corridor is on the Vision Zero Columbus High Injury Network due to the high incidence of serious and fatal crashes. The improvements will help to slow vehicle speeds and increase safety.

The project stems from the Joint Livingston Avenue Plan, a partnership with the City of Bexley to enhance safe travel along this area of the corridor. Grant funding is being pursued to make larger infrastructure improvements for safe multimodal travel.

Meanwhile, the city is working with the Driving Park community to address speeding and severe crashes on Livingston between 18th Street and Nelson Road. At a public meeting in November, preliminary concepts to design safer travel conditions were presented for feedback. The public can comment here.

The city has applied for a $12 million federal Safe Streets for All Implementation Grant to help fund design and construction of roadway improvements on this section of the Livingston corridor. Improvements will slow traffic speeds and enhance safety for all modes of travel.

New Employment with Public Service Means a Path Forward For Women Released from Marysville Reformatory 

A unique partnership between Public Service and the Ohio Reformatory for Women in Marysville is adding more women to the Department’s workforce — and offering an opportunity to help them rebuild their lives with skilled employment.

Currently, Public Service employs six women who graduated from the reformatory’s accredited vocational and horticulture programs. They earned certification for forklift, aerial lift, backhoe and flagging operations, plus workplace safety training.

These skills are a match for the Department’s entry-level positions such as laborer and maintenance worker. The women are also encouraged to complete our internal commercial driver’s license (CDL) program to be eligible for promotion to the city’s next job classification.

The six women are employed in our divisions of Infrastructure Management, Refuse Collection and Traffic Management. Two already have earned promotions.

Our Human Resources team interviews graduates and makes conditional job offers to qualified women before their release dates help set them up for post-release challenges, such as proof of income for housing.

Christina was hired by Public Service after her release in August and recently shared her story with WSYX-TV. Watch it here. 

“I’ve never been this happy before,” Christina said in the story.

Public Service HR Officer Lauren Hunter added, “They have a wonderful pool of well-qualified women who want to come out and work. This has been a wonderful match for us in terms of getting new employees, and it helps them by getting them stepped into a positive work environment.”

 

Department's Bridge Engineers Use Skills and Drone to Inspect Structural Safety

The Department’s Bridge Program provides vital services to ensure the safety of roadway and other bridges in the City of Columbus. Did you know our program maintains 209 Columbus bridges citywide and inspects a total of 310 bridges located within the city?

The additional inspection responsibilities cover structures that include railroad bridges and other privately-owned bridges spanning the public right of way. State law requires regular inspections.

Our bridge engineers in the Division of Infrastructure Management are trained and certified by ODOT to complete these inspections. Bridge Engineer Alina Gavrilov is an FAA Licensed Remote Pilot to operate the team’s drone. The new tool provides the team with greater access to bridge structures for inspection and data collection.

 

Public Service and The Ohio State University Partner to Assist Civil and Environmental Engineers of Tomorrow

To support diversity and interest in pursuing an engineering career with the city, the Department has pledged a $150,000 grant to The Ohio State University College of Engineering. The pledge will help establish the Columbus Transportation Leadership Endowed Fund to provide one or more scholarships to undergraduate students majoring in civil or environmental engineering.

Special consideration will be given to students interested in pursuing a public sector career in Central Ohio, and to students who are members of OSU organizations working to increase participation of historically underrepresented populations in the engineering profession.

“It is critical for the city to engage and empower future leaders in the engineering field, and it is an honor to support them,” said Public Service Director Jennifer Gallagher. “This endowment will help Columbus develop an equitable, diverse and talented group of engineers ready to solve complex mobility transportation challenges as we grow to a region of 3 million residents by 2050.”

This is the city’s first endowment at Ohio State. The university will match the $100,000 scholarship endowment. In addition, $50,000 of the Department’s grant will support Ohio State’s PREFACE program — Pre First-Year Academic and Career Engagement — to engage incoming first-year students in a summer enrichment program that presents challenges city engineers potentially are working to address.

2022 Litter League Teams Went to Bat to Keep Columbus Beautiful

The return this summer of Columbus Litter League scored a big win against litter in our community. More than 77,000 pounds of litter — 38.5 tons — was collected by Litter League members participating in 130 team cleanups.

A total of 31 teams registered in four divisions to clean up litter during the 2022 season from June through August. These committed volunteers collected 2,571 bags of litter!

Congratulations to the team in each division that collected the most bags of litter:

  • Corporate – Huntington Conservation Crew, 230 bags
  • Nonprofit – Clear Creeks & Byways, 224 bags
  • Community Groups – Southern Orchards Civic Association, 188 bags
  • Individuals – Captain Planet & The Planeteers, 171 bags

As the overall 2022 Litter League winner, the Huntington Conservation Crew earned the top prize of playing Wiffle ball on the Columbus Clippers field. And, in a friendly competition between Columbus and Toledo’s Litter League programs, our city earned the victory.

Litter League is managed by the Department’s Keep Columbus Beautiful program.

Scott Tourville and Justin Goodwin Are Named New Division Administrators 

Scott Tourville has joined the Department as the new Infrastructure Management Administrator.

He leads the division tasked with maintaining the city’s transportation infrastructure — from snow plowing, pothole patching and roadway repairs, to street sweeping, sidewalk repairs, roadside mowing and bridge maintenance. They also manage planning for the city’s street resurfacing program.

Scott previously served as City Engineer for the suburbs of Westerville and Pickerington. He is a licensed Professional Engineer who earned a bachelor’s degree in civil engineering from Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology and a master’s in public administration from Central Michigan University.

Justin Goodwin, who joined Public Service in 2018 as Transportation Planning Manager in our Division of Traffic Management, is the new Administrator of the Division of Mobility and Parking. With the city, Justin has been a leader in several multimodal and active transportation planning efforts focused on safe and equitable transportation in Columbus and Central Ohio, including LinkUS, Vision Zero and complete street design initiatives.

Justin is an American Institute of Certified Planner (AICP). He earned bachelor's and master's degrees in geography from Ohio University and a master’s in city and regional planning from The Ohio State University.

Resources

See a pothole? Let us know where and we’ll patch it.

Contact the 311 Service Center here.

Print the calendars or sign up to get reminders of your collection days.

item.title: City of Columbus to Host Pumpkin Drop-Off
item.description:
City of Columbus to Host First-Ever Pumpkin Drop-Off to Encourage Composting

Halloween generates a significant amount of organic waste from pumpkins and gourds that end up in our landfill. To help Columbus achieve our Climate Action Plan goals of reducing 90% of organic waste from our landfill and making our city a more sustainable community, we are excited to announce the first-ever pumpkin drop-off event this year.

It’s important that pumpkins do not mix with yard waste. Pumpkins do not decompose like grass clippings or leaves and are not acceptable for yard waste collection to avoid contaminating the waste stream.

To help with that, the city is providing a new service to residents this year. During November, residents may drop off their pumpkins and gourds at the Division of Refuse Collection Alum Creek Station to be composted.

What: City of Columbus Pumpkin Drop-Off

When: Nov. 1-30, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. (excluding Veterans Day and Thanksgiving Day)

Where: Division of Refuse Collection, 2100 Alum Creek, Columbus, Ohio 43207

Guidelines:

  • Intact and decaying pumpkins, carved jack-o’-lanterns and gourds only
  • No trash, food, recycling or other waste
  • Remove candles and any other non-organic items
  • Do not include pumpkins that have been painted or drawn on with permanent markers

If you can’t make it to our pumpkin composting drop-off, here are some alternative ways to help dispose of your pumpkins:

  • Feed local wildlife in the winter
  • Donate to local farms
  • Compost at home
  • As a last resort, toss them in the trash

Find more information and other drop-off sites throughout the region here.

item.title: Columbus Department of Public Service Newsletter Summer 2022
item.description:
From the Director's Desk

I hope you are enjoying the summer! It’s an especially active season for the Department of Public Service, as construction is in full swing on our infrastructure projects all around Columbus. You can catch up on a few in this newsletter, including our annual street resurfacing program. Visit the Public Service project page for more information on what is in construction this season.

The total reconstruction of Hudson Street through Linden is underway, as you'll see below. Infrastructure and pedestrian safety improvements we're making on Sullivant Avenue are nearing completion, and the new mural  painted in July on the I-70 underpass walls truly is "Sullivant Bright."

In Mayor Ginther’s 2022 capital improvements budget adopted in July by City Council, $30 million is included for the city's street resurfacing program to repair and repave more neighborhood streets throughout Columbus.

Overall, the Public Service 2022 capital budget has approximately $125 million in new funding and $85 million in carryover funding to invest in roadways, sidewalks, bikeways, bridges and other projects that deliver safe mobility and strengthen neighborhoods.

Speaking of bridges, the Department's $30 million project to rebuild Lazelle Road and the two railroad bridges spanning it in the Polaris area has achieved much-deserved industry recognition. Read more below about the recently completed undertaking.

Stay up to date on what's happening in all five Public Service divisions by following us on Twitter and Facebook. 

Sincerely,

Construction Has Started to Rebuild Hudson Street in Linden

Mayor Ginther joined city and Linden community leaders in July to officially kick off the rebuilding of Hudson Street from I-71 to Cleveland Avenue — a key east-west corridor infrastructure investment identified by the One Linden Community Plan.

The Mayor was also joined by several youth who participate in Remember Us Urban Scouts for mentorship and guidance in developing life skills, and whose monthly bike rides will be supported by the the project's improvements.

The $19 million reconstruction of Hudson will add a shared-use path on the south side of the street and sidewalk along the north side. The path is the first piece of the Central Ohio Greenways vision to create an east-west connection that ultimately links the Alum Creek Trail to the Olentangy Trail and the Scioto Trail.

Hudson will also get new waterline and storm sewers; new traffic signals, street lights and street trees; and improvements to the east leg of its intersection with I-71 to create a gateway to Linden.

Work is underway to install the waterline and reconstruct the roadway between Cleveland Avenue and McGuffey Road in the first phase, before the second phase starts from McGuffey to I-71. Anticipated completion of the full project is summer 2024.

During construction, traffic going eastbound on Hudson is being maintained. Westbound traffic is detoured to Weber Road. COTA bus stops have been temporarily relocated to Weber Road while construction is ongoing.

The City's Annual Street Resurfacing Program is Underway in Columbus Neighborhoods

In the city's two resurfacing projects this year, 162 streets are being repaved and 695 new Americans with Disabilities Act curb ramps are being installed at intersections along the streets.

Work is underway by the contractor to repave 91 streets in the first $14.5 million resurfacing project of this year's program, managed by our Department. Another contractor will start soon on the second project of nearly $8.7 million to resurface 71 streets. 

Resurfacing involves several steps by crews, including installing new ADA curb ramps and curb and sidewalk replacement for the ramps; milling existing pavement; making deep pavement repairs where needed; and laying the new pavement, first a tack coat that helps asphalt adhere to the roadway and then the final asphalt layer. Signage is posted to alert residents when temporary no parking must occur during a street’s resurfacing.

The Department’s program is a year-round effort built on continuous evaluation of maintenance needs and pavement conditions on streets citywide.

Click here for the list and map of streets to be paved in the city’s Resurfacing – 2022 Project 1 and Project 2.

Public Art + New Infrastructure Help to Reinvigorate Sullivant Avenue

Painting of the mural on the Sullivant Avenue I-70 underpass bridge walls finished in July, and the artwork illuminates the “intersections” of the community's history, communal tapestry and strong creative spirit.

Created by local artist Nick Stull, the mural is the showcase of the Sullivant Bright public art being incorporated with infrastructure and pedestrian safety improvements under construction on Sullivant Avenue from I-70 to Hague Avenue.

Stull and his team of artists completed the 8,400-square-foot mural one week ahead of schedule. Artistic lighting will be added to the underpass soon to complement the painting.

Stull titled the mural “Intersections” to highlight their importance, and to celebrate "the multifaceted intersections between people, infrastructure, environment and industry that create the unique communities of Sullivant Avenue."

Mayor Ginther’s $10 million investment to rehabilitate and upgrade the roadway, sidewalks, traffic signals, street lights, and pedestrian and aesthetic amenities will support safe mobility and lift up residents and businesses along the Sullivant corridor. Construction is expected to finish by the end of the year.

The mural and other Sullivant Bright permanent public art installations are part of the project.

Lazelle Road Reconstruction Project Earns Industry Accolades

The Lazelle Road reconstruction project to better support safe multimodal travel in the high-growth Polaris area recently earned industry recognition.

The massive $30 million project from US 23 to Worthington-Galena Road rebuilt and widened Lazelle, added a center turn lane and sidewalks and a shared-use path, and made drainage, street lighting and landscape improvements.

The South Old State Road intersection was relocated and a roundabout built for safer traffic flow and vehicle speeds, and a traffic signal was added at Flint Road. CSX and Norfolk Southern railroad bridges were demolished and replaced with new structures.

Three Ohio chapters of the Association for Bridge Construction and Design selected the project for the 2021 Short Span Railway Bridge Award as the best designed short-span railroad bridge in the state. The superstructure designs replaced the two old bridges of nearly 80 feet over Lazelle.

The project also earned the award for the 2021 ASHE Central Ohio Project of the Year Over $5 Million from the American Society of Highway Engineers.

At the ASHE National Conference, held in Columbus in May, the abstract Smart Expansion Beyond Last Generation: Lazelle Road Widening, was presented. The railroad bridges’ construction was also featured in the May issue of RT&S — Railway Track & Structures trade publication. 

Congratulations to our Division of Design and Construction project team and consultant partners for earning this recognition!

Refuse Collection Helped Ohio State University Students Go Green During Move Out/Move In

The Department’s Division of Refuse Collection supported students’ efforts to go green as they moved out of and into University District off-campus housing before the start of fall semester at The Ohio State University.

In a partnership with OSU's Office of Student Life and the University District Organization, the city for the first time added temporary dumpsters to collect recyclables and electronics recycling. Non-perishable food was accepted to donate to the Mid-Ohio Food Collective, and clothing donations were collected for local charities.

Refuse Collection traditionally has provided extra dumpsters at off-campus locations during OSU move out/move in to collect bulk items such as furniture, mattresses and rugs, and did so again this time. 

The recycling collection services that were added to support sustainability can help achieve the city’s Climate Action Plan strategies to reduce the amount of waste generated and increase the diversion rate from the landfill.

Conversion to Parking Kiosks Adds More Parking Payment Options

The Division of Parking Services has replaced nearly all city parking meters with new pay-by-plate kiosks to modernize and offer more payment options for on-street parking.

Now, you may use the ParkColumbus app to pay or scan to pay, text to pay, or call to pay with your mobile device. If you prefer to pay with coins or a debit or credit card, signage will direct you to the kiosk nearest where you park.

The transition in Downtown, the Brewery and University Districts and the Short North was completed before summer. A limited number of handicapped-accessible and 30-minute meters remain in place in some locations.

Find more helpful tips here or by following the My Buddy Charles video series here.  

Interested in getting an old parking meter? Parking Services has a limited supply available. Email parkingservices@columbus.gov to share your interest.

The Department's Construction Inspectors Bring Skilled Oversight to Public and Private Infrastructure Projects

Construction inspectors in the Division of Design and Construction inspect and oversee building of the city’s capital improvement and private infrastructure projects like roadways, sidewalks, bridges, ADA curb ramps and utility lines installation.

Our team performs daily inspections on the city’s large capital projects — in 2021, the division managed more than 50 active capital projects valued at approximately $250 million. Our Private Construction Inspectors annually perform more than 15,000 inspections. The Testing Section inspectors support all infrastructure construction by providing concrete, asphalt, pipe, earthwork and aggregate testing.

Design and Construction inspectors work to ensure that procedures and materials comply with infrastructure projects’ plans, specifications and standard drawings.

Resources

See a pothole? Tell us, and we’ll fix it. Report the location to the 311 Service Center at https://www.columbus.gov/311/, by email here or call (614) 645-3111.

If you see illegal dumping in a city alley, please report it to 311.

Refuse Collection Solid Waste Investigators work to hold offenders accountable.

Get street sweeping schedules and reminders here.

Street sweeping season is still underway.

item.title: City of Columbus to Resurface 71 More Neighborhood Streets
item.description:
For Immediate Release

July 21, 2022

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

City of Columbus to Repave 71 More Streets in Second 2022 Resurfacing Package

The City of Columbus will repave another 71 city streets in the second phase of its 2022 resurfacing program, bringing the total investment this year for the annual capital improvements project to more than $23 million.

This phase includes installation of 299 new Americans with Disabilities Act curb ramps at intersections along the 71 streets to be resurfaced. Combined with the first 2022 resurfacing project contract of $14.5 million approved in June, 162 city streets will be paved and 695 new ADA ramps constructed.

“We appreciate how important a safe and smooth street surface is to our residents as they drive, bike and walk in their neighborhoods,” said Jennifer L. Gallagher, Director of the Department of Public Service. “Street resurfacing is an important capital investment made by the city each year to support safe mobility throughout our community.”  

At its meeting on Monday, City Council authorized an $8.68 million contract with Strawser Paving to resurface the second package of streets. The project includes pedestrian safety improvements and traffic calming installation on two streets identified as in need by Vision Zero Columbus based on location and conditions.

On Bryden Road, curb extensions will be built at intersections from 17th Avenue to Fairwood Avenue to help slow vehicle speeds, increase visibility of pedestrians and shorten the distance to cross the street. Speed humps will be installed on Atcheson Street from St. Clair Avenue to Taylor Avenue; they already exist on Atcheson east of the new installation set to occur.

“Whether you’re on two feet, two wheels, four or more, our city is investing in transportation infrastructure improvements to ensure safe travel by all modes,” said City Councilmember Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, chair of the Public Service and Transportation Committee.

Click here for a list and map of the 71 streets to be paved in the city’s Resurfacing – 2022 Project 2.

item.title: City of Columbus to Launch Rideshare Pick Up/Drop Off Zones Pilot
item.description:
For Immediate Release

July 13, 2022

Contact: Debbie Briner, Department of Public Service

614-645-6467; dsbriner@columbus.gov

Contact: Becca Goodburn, Deputy Director, Affinity & Advancement, Short North Alliance, 614-299-8050; info@shortnorth.org

 

Web – Facebook – Twitter

City of Columbus to Launch Short North Pilot to Support Rideshare User Safety

The City of Columbus is partnering with the Short North Alliance, COTA, Lyft and Uber on a pilot program to designate late night drop-off and pickup zones that support safe, convenient mobility for rideshare users visiting the popular arts district.

Beginning on Friday, July 15, the eight marked zones designated along High Street between 4th Street and Goodale Street will operate daily from 10 p.m. to 3 a.m. The zones, marked off by Late Night Rideshare Pick Up and Drop Off signage, will temporarily operate at COTA bus stop locations that are not currently in use by buses during those hours. 

“The pilot program will present the opportunity to create a safer environment to manage rideshare use and traffic flow along High Street in the busy Short North,” said Jennifer L. Gallagher, Director of the Columbus Department of Public Service. “It offers another potential tool to support mobility options in our city and safely manage high curb demand.”

“Rideshare options are extremely convenient and help patrons avoid driving while under the influence. However, we recognize that they can still pose safety concerns with increased traffic stopping on High Street,” said Betsy Pandora, Executive Director of the Short North Alliance. “This pilot program is one step we are taking to support the safety and wellbeing of visitors leveraging these transportation options.”

Those who are using Lyft or Uber rideshare services when visiting the Short North will be directed by the service app to the nearest drop-off/pickup zone. The rideshare driver will be notified that a customer is waiting in that zone for a ride.

The pilot is set to operate through Oct. 15 and then be evaluated by the program’s partners.

Columbus Public Service Changes Due to Independence Day

Trash Collection:

City of Columbus trash collection service will not be provided on Monday, July 4, in observance of Independence Day.

For residents assigned a collection color, pickup will rotate forward by one day the week of the holiday:

Monday, July 4:                          NO COLLECTION

Tuesday, July 5:                         Gold

Wednesday, July 6:                   Gray   

Thursday, July 7:                       Navy

Friday, July 8:                             Pink

Monday, July 11:                       Ruby      

The color-coded trash collection schedule will rotate forward again on Labor Day, Monday, Sept. 5.

For residents not assigned a collection color: If your collection day falls on or after the holiday, your trash pickup will be delayed by one day during the week of the holiday.

Recycling and Yard Waste Collection: Biweekly recycling and yard waste service with a collection day that falls on or after the holiday will be delayed by one day during the week of the holiday, with Friday’s collection occurring on Saturday.  Drop-Off Options: For recycling drop-off locations see https://recycleright.org/recycling locations/?category=49; for yard waste drop-off locations see: http://www.columbus.gov/publicservice/refuse-collection/Yard-Waste-Collection/ or contact the 311 Service Center online at https://www.columbus.gov/311/, by email at 311@columbus.gov or at (614) 645-3111.

Residents can check their collection days and set collection schedule reminders on our website at www.columbus.gov/publicservice/Refuse-Collection/.

Parking Kiosks and Meters: Motorists may park free of charge at kiosks and meters on Monday, July 4. Parking restriction signage at some meters will be enforced, including but not limited to morning and evening rush hours and zones marked for valets, taxis, loading, handicapped-only and residential parking permit areas.

Offices Closed: Department offices, including the Parking Violations Bureau and the Right-of-Way Permits Office, will be closed on Monday, July 4. Permits may be filed online at https://ca.columbus.gov/ca/

item.description:
For Immediate Release

June 28, 2022

Contact: Debbie Briner

614-645-6467

dsbriner@columbus.gov

Street Closures and Parking Restrictions Set for Red, White & Boom

Street closures and on-street parking restrictions will occur in downtown Columbus this week to prepare for Red, White & Boom on Friday, July 1.

Street closures include:

  • Washington Blvd from Broad St. to Main St. currently is closed.
  • Civic Center Dr. from Broad St. to Main St. will close Wednesday at 9 a.m. through Saturday.
  • Spring St. from Neil Ave. to Marconi Blvd. will close Thursday at 9 a.m. through Saturday at 6 a.m.
    • Note: Spring St. will have one lane open on Thursday and Friday evenings for rush hour leaving downtown, 4 to 6 p.m.
  • Long St. from Hocking St. to Marconi Blvd. will close Thursday at 9 a.m. through Saturday at 6 a.m.
    • Note: Long St. will have one lane open on Thursday and Friday mornings for rush hour coming downtown, 6 to 9 a.m.
  • Marconi Blvd. from Long St. to Broad St. will close Thursday at 5 p.m. through Saturday at 6 a.m.
  • Several downtown streets will close Friday at 2 p.m. for the Red, White & Boom parade to form, with additional street closures occurring during the parade from approximately 5 p.m. until 7:30 p.m. 
  • For the fireworks, all streets in the area bounded by Spring St. on the north, 3rd St. on the east, Mound St. on the south and McDowell St. on the west will close Friday from 5:30 p.m. through midnight.

A street closures map and complete details can be viewed here.

View this map for on-street parking restrictions taking effect this week throughout the downtown business district. Most of the restrictions will begin after 10 p.m. Thursday and last until 6 a.m. Saturday. Look for temporary “no stopping” signs that will be put in place 24 hours in advance.

The ParkColumbus mobile payment app will remind users before they activate a parking session about the Red, White & Boom parking restrictions. The reminder message will appear on the app from 6 a.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday.
